title: 7 smart reasons to sell a stock—and my ‘golden rule’ for offloading shares, says hedge fund CEO
description: Nobody is born knowing anything innately about the stock market. And if you feel like you've missed the investing class, you didn't. Usually there isn
body: Nobody is born knowing anything innately about the stock market. And if you feel like you've missed the investing class, you didn't. Usually there isn't one. So responsible people who are trying to do the responsible thing by building a portfolio for themselves and their families often find huge gaps in their knowledge and don't know where to turn. As the co-founder and CEO of the hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money, I know that there's no shortage of advice when you're getting started about great investments to buy. It can feel easy and gratifying, especially when your portfolio is doing well. But then things get tougher.One of the hardest things to do as an investor is to figure out when to sell. You buy a stock because you believe it will go up in value. But the decision to sell is rarely so straightforward. Personally, I've made just about every selling mistake. But over time, I've developed a framework for knowing when to sell — and when not to. Why selling is so hard Selling decisions are often rooted in emotion and cognitive bias rather than logic. One major culprit: anchoring to past performance, a flawed reference point that clouds clear thinking. Behavioral economics, particularly prospect theory, shows that we experience the pain of a loss more intensely than the joy of a gain. This leads investors to cling to losers ("just need to get back to even") and sell winners too early ("lock in the gain"). We also place too much emphasis on recent events, a phenomenon known as recency bias. If your last tech stock soared, you're more likely to chase another. If your last trade flopped, you may avoid the market altogether. And when recent trades go well, people tend to trade more — often to their detriment. Finally, selling triggers a storm of second-guessing and rationalization. Here are my responses to common excuses: "What if I'm wrong and it goes up?" What if you're right and it keeps going down? "What will I do with the cash?" You don't always need to put it to work right away, or you can buy a little more of what you already own. "If I double down and it rebounds, I'll make it all back." But if it continues to go down from here, your losses will double. "I don't like having a loss, so I'll sell once it gets back to even." What you originally paid is irrelevant. Yet for many investors, it becomes the most important factor in their decision-making. To assuage their fragile egos, they risk even bigger losses. 7 smart reasons to sell a stockThese biases and emotional landmines are why you need a clear, disciplined plan for when to sell, including when:The original thesis no longer holds. If the fundamental reasons you bought the stock are no longer true — if earnings slow, revenue shrinks, margins deteriorate or the company loses market share — it may be time to move on.  There's a regulatory risk. Legislative changes can dramatically shift a company's prospects. For example, the outlook for solar-related companies can decline dramatically when tax credits are cut for installations. Management loses credibility. Frequent earnings misses or misleading guidance suggest deeper problems. One-off surprises happen; recurring surprises reflect poor leadership. It becomes too big a slice of your portfolio. A stock that grows from 10% to 25% of your portfolio due to the superb performance of its underlying business, which fuels a soaring stock price, increases your risk from a diversification standpoint. Rebalancing is smart and necessary. The maximum I would have in any one position in my own portfolio is 20% — and that's probably too much! The stock becomes overvalued. Sometimes the hype drives prices beyond what fundamentals justify. If valuation detaches from reality, it's okay to take some profits. If it really goes nuts, I will sell enough to take my original investment off the table. You need the money elsewhere. Selling to fund a home, college tuition or retirement is perfectly valid. Opportunity cost matters. You have tax reasons. For example, tax-loss harvesting may allow you to offset capital gains or deduct up to $3,000 of losses against ordinary income. My golden rule of sellingWhen you've decided to sell for a solid reason — especially the first, second, or third outlined above — don't hesitate. Don't wait for the perfect price. Just sell. When not to sell Just as important as knowing when to sell is knowing when not to sell. Avoid emotionally driven decisions that sabotage long-term gains. Don't sell just because it went up. Great companies like Costco, Apple and Microsoft have rewarded patience for decades. Selling too early can mean missing out on compounding returns. Don't sell just because it went down. Market pullbacks are often temporary. If the fundamentals are intact and the decline is market driven, it may be a buying opportunity rather than a reason to exit. Trying to time the market rarely ends well. Don't sell because of scary headlines. Economic fears are often priced in before they fully materialize. The market is, forward-looking; headlines usually aren't. Selling during fear often means missing the rebound. Selling well is an advanced investing skill that demands discipline, logic and self-awareness, and there's no place for ego. If you create a sound game plan, you'll be equipped to act confidently, even in the face of uncertainty. I keep a list of reasons to sell handy so I can literally look at it and keep my wits about me. Karen Finerman is co-founder and CEO of the New York-based hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money. She is the author of the New York Times bestselling book, "Finerman's Rules: Secrets I'd Only Tell My Daughters About Business and Life" and the host of the podcast How She Does It. Karen is a proud member of the Wharton Board of Advisors, her alma mater, and serves on the board of The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research.

schema.headline: 7 smart reasons to sell a stock—and my ‘golden rule’ for offloading shares, says hedge fund CEO

title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months
description: Alberto Musalem, President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, speaks to the Economic Club of New York, in New York City, U.S., Feb. 20,
body: Alberto Musalem, President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, speaks to the Economic Club of New York, in New York City, U.S., Feb. 20, 2025.Brendan McDermid | ReutersSt. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation.During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case  that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity."The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said.Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April.Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028.To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed. "Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows.However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target, thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%."It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."

schema.headline: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months

title: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets
description: Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media re
body: Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump's tax statements.The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.Epstein, Russia and TrumpDeutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported. Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconDeutsche Bank.The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. Fresh scrutinyThe reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny. The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years."Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025."Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

schema.headline: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets

title: Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO
description: Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis speaks at the 2026 Google I/O technology developer conference in Mountain View, California, May 19, 2026.Karl Mondon
body: Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis speaks at the 2026 Google I/O technology developer conference in Mountain View, California, May 19, 2026.Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty ImagesIsomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the company said on Tuesday.Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014.The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet, Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI.Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology. Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021."When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," said Hassabis."This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added.Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines.Anthropic announced it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April.Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure.Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.

schema.headline: Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO

title: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersPrediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersPrediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday. Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast.  Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments. Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month.The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk. A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025. "The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson. In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order. In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied.A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000.Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets. In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues. As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request

title: Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz
description: Douglas Rissing | Istock | Getty ImagesPolitical advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a mi
body: Douglas Rissing | Istock | Getty ImagesPolitical advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.Spending by partyThe 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns. The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis. Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact. While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%. Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas. It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans. Spending by mediumWhile party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed. Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming. Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

schema.headline: Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks
description: A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer's pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesThe U.S.
body: A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer's pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesThe U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement. "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement. In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response." "We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported. Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

schema.headline: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

title: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’
description: This combination of pictures created on November 17, 2026 shows (bottom) a grab taken from a video released on November 17, 2026 by the Ukrainian Secu
body: This combination of pictures created on November 17, 2026 shows (bottom) a grab taken from a video released on November 17, 2026 by the Ukrainian Security Service showing the damaged after a strike Crimean bridge (Kerch bridge) and (top) a view of the bridge taken on October 14, 2022. - AFP | Getty ImagesUkraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure.Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days.Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved."Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X."We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added.Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported.Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.  A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory.Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section. Russia attacks Kyiv infrastructureThe co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point, Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike."We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea. In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with member of the Presidium of the Political Bureau and secretary of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea at the Kremlin in Moscow on November 16, 2026.Kristina Solovyova | Afp | Getty ImagesRussian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv. Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges. Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies.The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday.Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out. "Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.

schema.headline: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’

title: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing
description: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesFede
body: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesFederal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.The committee established last month by President Donald Trump, who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf."Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett.Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing."Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote."Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden. Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

schema.headline: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing

title: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations
description: Home Depot store logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 3, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesHome Depot on Tuesday
body: Home Depot store logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 3, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesHome Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said. "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan."McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles. "We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results. The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expectedRevenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expectedThe company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period."We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts.In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase. Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

schema.headline: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations

title: Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years
description: A Nike Inc. store in the Colaba district of Mumbai, India, Oct. 12, 2025.Abeer Khan | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike said Tuesday ahead of its first inv
body: A Nike Inc. store in the Colaba district of Mumbai, India, Oct. 12, 2025.Abeer Khan | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance. The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve.""What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said. He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China. Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year. Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027. The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers. At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years. He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India. "If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said. CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises. Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

schema.headline: Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years

title: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC
description: A Nvidia sign is displayed at the company's headquarters on November 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, California.Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images News | Getty I
body: A Nvidia sign is displayed at the company's headquarters on November 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, California.Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesNvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.Read more CNBC tech newsAnthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBCDemis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEOOpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company’s safety workHow Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time offSeparately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.Nvidia under pressureOn Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stands on the red carpet at the Invest In Germany Summit to announce a strategic cooperation between the German government, Nvidia and a group of German companies in artificial intelligence capacity for German industry on Oct. 19, 2026, in Berlin.Nadja Wohlleben | Getty ImagesBessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls."I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.In an August securities filing, Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

schema.headline: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC

title: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout
description: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapse
body: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down big the last month and a half. According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy. Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast.It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.Aschenbrenner — who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.The Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off. The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.Stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology. Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised."Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company.Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

schema.headline: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout

title: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
description: watch nowSentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and l
body: watch nowSentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020."Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them."The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23. title: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
description: Travelers use Delta bag check kiosks at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Georgia, Nov. 14, 2026.Elijah Nouvelage | Bloombe
body: Travelers use Delta bag check kiosks at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Georgia, Nov. 14, 2026.Elijah Nouvelage | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.  Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong. "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat. The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment. Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades."I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.watch now

schema.headline: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
